overview:
Rachel, still childless, gives Jacob her maid Bilhah, who bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah answers with her maid Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Reuben finds mandrakes, and Rachel buys them from Leah with a night with Jacob; Leah conceives Issachar, then Zebulun, then a daughter, Dinah. At last God remembers Rachel, and she bears Joseph. Jacob then asks to go home. Laban asks him to name his wages, and Jacob asks only for the speckled, spotted, and dark animals born from now on. Laban removes all such animals, but Jacob's peeled rods and selective breeding make the marked young many and strong, and Jacob grows rich.

Every son gets a name with a reason, spoken by his mother. The names record the sisters' rivalry as it happens: “With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister” (v. 8). The chapter turns at Joseph's birth (v. 25), when the story shifts from wives to wages.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The patriarchal age, traditionally c. 2000–1700 BC. Joseph's birth ends Jacob's fourteen years of service for his wives; the flock bargain covers the last six years (31:41).

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. The naming speeches play on the Hebrew sound of each name.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Laban's household and pastures near Haran in Paddan-aram.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jacob's sons listed by mother in 35:23–26 and 46:8–27. D&C 132:34, 37 compares Sarah's giving Hagar to Abraham and counts Jacob's marriages as commanded.

hermeneutics:
A barren wife could give her husband a slave woman to bear children for her, and the practice appears in law and contract. Hammurabi's laws assume it and protect the wife's rank: the slave who has borne children may not claim equality with her mistress (§§144–147). A Nuzi adoption contract (HSS 5 67) requires a childless wife to provide a slave woman and gives the wife authority over the children. Rachel's words fit this world. Bilhah will bear “upon my knees,” and Rachel says, literally, “I shall be built up” from her (v. 3), the same phrase Sarah used of Hagar (16:2). The sons count as Rachel's and Leah's, which is why the mothers, not the maids, name them.

Mandrakes were famous in the ancient world as a love charm. Theophrastus (4th century BC) reports that the root was used for love potions and that those who dug it were told to speak of love while cutting. The Hebrew *duda'im* sounds like *dodim*, “love,” and the Song of Songs pairs mandrakes with lovers' gifts (Song 7:13). Rachel wants them as a fertility aid. The story's answer is pointed: Leah, who gave the mandrakes away, conceives, and Rachel conceives only when “God remembered Rachel” (v. 22).

In the Levant most sheep were white and most goats dark; the Song of Songs pictures hair like a flock of goats and teeth like newly washed sheep (Song 4:1–2). Jacob's request for only the speckled and dark-marked animals sounded like a tiny wage, which is why Laban agrees at once (v. 34).

breakdown.label: Rachel's envy; Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali
Leah's answer; Zilpah bears Gad and Asher
Reuben's mandrakes traded for a night
Leah bears Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah
Jacob asks to leave; the speckled-flock wage
Laban removes the marked animals three days away
Peeled rods and stronger flocks; Jacob grows rich

structure.summary: Births, then wages, joined at Joseph's birth. Inside the chapter no strong pattern; it moves in sequence. The chapter holds the center of a chiasm that Fishbane and Rendsburg trace across the whole Jacob cycle.

notes: **Naming formula:** “called his name” occurs 12 times from 29:32 to 30:24, for eleven sons and Dinah. Leah's first speeches call on “the LORD” (YHWH); from 30:2 to 30:23 the narrative says “God” (*Elohim*) nine times, and “the LORD” returns only in Joseph's name (v. 24).

**Hire:** the root *s-k-r* (“hire,” “wages”) occurs 6 times: Leah has “hired” Jacob with the mandrakes (v. 16, twice) and names Issachar for her “hire” (v. 18); then Jacob bargains for his own “hire” (vv. 28, 32, 33).
**Wordplay:** Laban's name is the Hebrew for “white,” and Jacob beats him by peeling white streaks (*lavan*) in rods of poplar (*livneh*, v. 37).

The birth account runs from 29:31 to 30:24; the wage story starts at v. 25 and carries into ch. 31, where Laban's sons complain that Jacob has taken their father's wealth (31:1). Benjamin, the twelfth son, is born only after the return, on the road near Bethlehem (35:16–19).

**Echoes:** the sons named here become the tribes of Israel (49:1–28). Rachel, who cried “Give me children, or else I die” (v. 1), dies giving birth to Benjamin (35:16–19); Jeremiah 31:15 hears her weeping for her children.

traditions.text: Explains Sarah's giving Hagar to Abraham as obedience to God's law and says Abraham was not under condemnation for it. It goes on to say that Isaac and Jacob “did none other things than that which they were commanded,” which places Rachel's and Leah's gifts of their maids in the same light. Genesis itself only reports the rivalry.

Dates every birth to the day and year, so that the sons' births overlap across the four mothers; Reuben comes first, and Joseph's birth falls in the same year as Zebulun's. It makes Zebulun and Dinah twins and says Leah gave Issachar to a nurse. Jacob's wage is the lambs and kids born black, spotted, and white, and Laban and his sons, envious, take back the sheep and watch Jacob with evil intent.

Gives each name a meaning for Greek readers: Dan is “divine judgment,” Naphtali “unconquerable in stratagems,” since Rachel outwitted her sister's fruitfulness, Gad “fortune,” and Issachar one “born by hire.” Reuben brings “apples of mandrakes,” Rachel longs to eat them, and she yields Jacob for the night to soften her sister's anger. Josephus also insists the maids were by no means slaves, though subject to their mistresses.

Issachar tells his own birth story. Rachel did not eat the mandrakes but offered them in the house of the Lord, and God gave her two sons because she wanted Jacob for the sake of children, not pleasure. Leah's six sons and Rachel's two are thus both explained by the mandrakes. Augustine, centuries later, also doubted the fruit had any power.

Records disagreement over what *duda'im* were: mandrakes, barley, or the fruit of a tree. All agree Reuben picked only from ownerless land, since it was harvest and he would not take another's grain, and that he brought them to his mother before tasting them. Rashi identifies the plant as violets, called jasmine in Arabic.

Explains the rods as working through sight: the ewe saw the peeled rods at the trough, startled, and bore young that looked like them. The rabbis illustrate with a story of an Ethiopian couple who had a white son, explained by white portraits in their house. Rabbi Huna offers another cause, reading 31:12 to mean that angels carried rams from Laban's flock into Jacob's.

Reads Dinah's name, from *din* “judgment,” as Leah's verdict on herself. Knowing twelve tribes would come from Jacob and that she and the maids had already borne ten, she reasoned that another son would leave Rachel with fewer than a maid. Her unborn child was changed to a daughter. Rashi adds that Rachel, naming Joseph, asked for just one more son for the same reason.

Dates the mandrakes to the month of Sivan, at wheat harvest. Its version of Dinah's birth goes further than the Talmud's: after Leah's prayer the unborn children were exchanged, Joseph given to Rachel's womb and Dinah to Leah's. When Joseph is born, Jacob says by the Holy Spirit that the house of Joseph will be a flame to consume the house of Esau, an echo of Obadiah 18, and so he no longer fears Esau.

Reads the two flocks as two kinds of mind. Laban's flock “devoid of all distinctive marks” is matter without quality, and the uneducated soul that takes such matter for its gods. Jacob presides over the marked and many-colored flock, the mind that has been shaped by learning and knows that a Creator stamped every species with its form.

Reads the many-colored sheep as Christ's wages: people of every nation gathered into one company of faith, as the Father promised the Son the nations for his inheritance (Psalm 2:8). Jacob's sons by two sisters and two maids show that Christ raises up children of God from free and slave alike, giving all the same Spirit. Justin had already made the speckled-sheep comparison.

Reports that he once saw a mandrake and examined it by sight, smell, and taste: a nice-looking, sweet-smelling, but insipid fruit. He doubts it makes barren women fruitful, since Leah, not Rachel, conceived after the trade, and Leah bore two more children before God opened Rachel's womb. He then reads the fruit as good reputation, which the scholar must earn by taking up active work.
